points: Gentius was an Illyrian king.
Gentius belonged to the Labeatan dynasty.
The Ancient Greek form of his name was Γένθιος (Génthios).
Gentius reigned from 181 to 168 BC.
The article introduces Gentius as the last attested Illyrian king.
Gentius was the son and successor of Pleuratus III.
Pleuratus III maintained friendly relations with Rome.
Scodra was the capital of the Illyrian kingdom under Gentius.
Scodra is now Shkodër, Albania.
The Dalmatae, formerly subjects of the kingdom, declared independence in 180 BC, early in Gentius's reign.
The Daorsi, also formerly subjects of the kingdom, declared independence in 180 BC.
Rhizon abandoned Gentius before his defeat.
The Romans granted Rhizon immunity.
Gentius married Etuta.
Etuta was the daughter of the Dardanian king Monunius II.
In 171 BC, Gentius sided with Rome against Macedonia.
In 169 BC, Gentius switched sides and allied with Perseus of Macedon.
Lissus was the southernmost city of Gentius's kingdom.
Lissus is now Lezhë, Albania.
Lissus had marked the kingdom's southern limit since the First Illyrian War.
Gentius arrested two Roman envoys.
Gentius accused the Roman envoys of being spies rather than emissaries.
The introduction says Gentius destroyed Apollonia.
The introduction says Gentius destroyed Epidamnos.
Apollonia was allied with Rome.
Epidamnos was allied with Rome.
Epidamnos was called Dyrrachium by the Romans.
Epidamnos is now Durrës, Albania.
A Roman force under Lucius Anicius Gallus defeated Gentius at Scodra in 168 BC.
The introduction gives twenty or thirty days as the time it took Rome to defeat Gentius.
Gentius was brought to Rome as a captive in 167 BC.
Gentius appeared as a captive in Gallus's triumph.
Gentius was eventually held at Iguvium after the triumph.
The date of Gentius's death is unknown.
After defeating Gentius, Rome divided the region into three administrative divisions called meris.
The extent of the first meris is unknown.
The second meris was Labeates.
The third meris included Acruvium, Rhizon, Olcinium, and their surroundings.
The Illyrian name Gentius appears to derive from the Proto-Indo-European root *ǵenh₁-, meaning 'to beget'.
The proposed root is also reflected in the Latin gens, gentis, meaning 'kin, clan, race'.
The article reconstructs the noun behind Gentius as *gent(i)yos.
The reconstructed noun is said to designate the king as the head of his kin.
The article compares the reconstructed noun with Proto-Germanic *kun-ing-az.
The article suggests that the Albanian name Gjin may derive from Gentius.
If that derivation is correct, the name changed form and was Christianized.
Relations between Rome and the Ardiaean state deteriorated under Gentius.
Rome had controlled the coast and hinterland south of the Drin since the First Illyrian War against Teuta.
Gentius sought greater control over related peoples to the north and west.
Issa was a Greek island city.
Issa retained some independence under Roman protection.
Issa is now Vis, Croatia.
Pharos remained an Illyrian possession during Gentius's reign.
Pharos is now Hvar, Croatia.
Illyrian military strength lay chiefly in its fleet.
Illyrian interference with Adriatic shipping renewed Roman interest in the area.
In 180 BC, a Roman praetor arrived at Brudisium with some of Gentius's ships.
The praetor was responsible for coastal protection.
The ships brought to Brudisium were said to have been caught committing piracy.
A Roman embassy to Illyria could not locate Gentius.
The praetor discovered that Romans were being held for ransom at Korčula.
No outcome of the 180 BC affair is reported.
Gentius's envoys claimed that the charges against him were false.
The Roman Senate may have accepted the envoys' denial.
About ten years after the piracy affair, Rome was eager for war against Perseus.
Around that time, Issa accused Gentius of plotting war with Perseus.
The Roman Senate refused to hear the Illyrian envoys after Issa's accusation.
Rome seized 54 Illyrian lembi anchored in the harbor of Epidamnos.
On the eve of war, Rome sent a senator to remind Gentius of his formal friendship with the Roman Republic.
In 169 BC, Gentius arranged the murder of his brother Plator.
Etuta had been engaged to Plator.
Gentius had Plator killed because he believed that marrying Etuta would make Plator too powerful.
Gentius married Etuta after having Plator killed.
Marrying Etuta secured Gentius an alliance with the Dardani.
The Dardani were a powerful people.
Perseus recaptured several Roman outposts in Roman-occupied Illyria.
By retaking the outposts, Perseus gained control of the westward route to the Ardiaean state.
Perseus sent his first embassy to Gentius after securing that route.
The Illyrian exile Pleuratus was part of Perseus's first embassy.
The article also lists the Macedonian Adaeus and Beroea in its account of the embassy's composition.
Perseus's first embassy found Gentius at Lissos, another form of Lissus.
The embassy told Gentius of Perseus's successes against Rome.
The embassy told Gentius of Perseus's successes against the Dardani.
The embassy told Gentius of Perseus's recent victory over the Penestae.
Gentius indicated that he was willing to fight Rome.
Gentius said he lacked the money to fight Rome.
Perseus's first embassy made no promise of money.
Perseus sent another embassy from Stuberra shortly afterward.
The embassy from Stuberra also made no promise of money.
Perseus kept trying to bring Gentius into the war.
Perseus reportedly hoped to enlist Gentius without spending any of his own treasury.
The Illyrian exile Pleuratus, also spelled Plearatus in the article, raised 1,000 infantry from the Penestae.
Pleuratus also raised 200 cavalry from the Penestae.
Rome invaded Macedonia in 168 BC.
The invasion forced Perseus to promise Gentius a subsidy.
Gentius's ships could be used against Rome.
The subsidy under discussion was 300 talents.
Perseus sent his companion Pantauchus to arrange the agreement.
The two sides agreed on hostages at Meteon.
Meteon is now Medun, Montenegro.
Gentius accepted Perseus's oath at Meteon.
Gentius sent Olympio with a delegation to collect the money from Perseus.
The treaty was concluded ceremonially at Dium.
Dium was on the Thermaic Gulf.
The Macedonians held a formal cavalry parade.
The cavalry parade may have impressed the Illyrians.
The cavalry may have represented the Macedonians in the treaty's ratification.
The 300 talents were counted out from the royal treasury at Pella.
The Illyrians were allowed to mark the money with their own stamp.
Pantauchus handed over an advance of ten talents to Gentius.
When the advance was handed over, Gentius was urged to begin hostilities against Rome.
The Roman envoys arrested by Gentius had been sent by Appius Claudius at Lychnidus.
Perseus recalled the rest of the subsidy after Gentius imprisoned the Roman envoys.
Perseus withheld the rest of the money because he believed the arrests had committed Gentius to the alliance regardless of payment.
Gentius took measures to strengthen his state as he turned against Rome.
Gentius centralized his finances by imposing a single tax on all his subjects.
Gentius took royal control of the mint at Lissus.
Gentius took royal control of the mint at Scodra.
Gentius resided at Lissus.
Gentius also resided at Scodra.
Gentius issued bronze coins.
The Selcë hoard contains two coins of Gentius bearing Macedonian emblems.
Other coins probably depict Gentius's head.
The probable portrait shows a cap resembling a petasos.
The probable portrait shows a torque around his head.
One of these coins shows a thunderbolt on the reverse.
The others show a lembus warship on the reverse.
A Roman inventory put the prewar Illyrian treasury's gold at 27 pounds.
The inventory put the treasury's silver at 19 pounds.
The inventory listed 120,000 Illyrian drachmas.
The inventory listed 13,000 Roman denarii.
Gentius and Perseus sent a joint embassy inviting Rhodes to join the war against Rome.
Gentius built up a fleet of 270 lembi.
The fleet indicated that Gentius expected to face an enemy in the Adriatic.
Gentius had an army of 15,000 men.
The article describes Gentius as ready for war with Rome after these preparations.
Gentius assembled his army and fleet at Lissus.
In January or February 168 BC, Gentius advanced into Roman territory.
Gentius besieged the Illyrian city of Bassania.
Bassania was allied with Rome.
Bassania refused to surrender to Gentius.
Bassania was only five miles from Lissus.
Caravantius was Gentius's half-brother.
Caravantius took 1,000 infantry on a separate expedition.
Caravantius also took 50 horsemen.
Caravantius attacked the Cavii.
Caravantius failed to capture one of the Cavii's cities.
Caravantius ravaged the fields of Caravandis.
A flotilla of eight Illyrian lembi set out a little later to attack Epidamnos and Apollonia.
Epidamnos and Apollonia were coastal colonial cities.
Appius Claudius learned that Gentius had allied with Perseus.
Appius Claudius learned that Gentius had arrested the Roman envoys.
In response, Appius Claudius moved his army out of winter quarters at Nymphaeum.
Appius Claudius gathered troops from Byllis, Epidamnos, and Apollonia as he marched north.
Appius Claudius encamped by the river Genesus.
The Genesus is now the Shkumbin River in Albania.
Appius Claudius met the new Roman commander, Lucius Anicius Gallus, at the Genesus.
Lucius Anicius Gallus was a praetor.
Anicius crossed from Italy to Apollonia with two legions.
Anicius's two legions included 600 cavalry.
Anicius's two legions included 10,400 infantry.
Rome's Italian allies contributed 800 cavalry.
Rome's Italian allies contributed 10,000 infantry.
The size of Anicius's fleet is unknown.
Anicius reinforced his fleet with 5,000 sailors.
The Parthini were an Illyrian koinon allied with Rome.
The Parthini added 200 cavalry to Anicius's force.
The Parthini added 2,000 infantry to Anicius's force.
The combined Roman-led forces outnumbered Gentius's forces two to one.
Little is known about the campaign because a leaf of Livy's text is missing.
Anicius's fleet appears to have fought the Illyrians at sea.
Anicius's fleet apparently captured a number of Illyrian lembi.
The Romans then defeated the Illyrians on land.
The land victory allowed the Romans to advance into the heart of Illyrian territory.
The Romans secured most enemy cities' surrenders through negotiation rather than direct assault.
Gentius concentrated his remaining troops near Scodra.
Scodra was well fortified.
Scodra occupied a naturally defensible position.
Anicius approached Scodra with his army in battle formation.
The Illyrians panicked and fled into Scodra as Anicius approached.
Gentius asked Anicius for a three-day truce.
Anicius granted the truce.
Gentius hoped Caravantius would arrive with a large relief army during the truce.
The expected relief army did not arrive.
After his defeat, Gentius sent Teuticus and Bellus to negotiate with Anicius.
Teuticus and Bellus were prominent tribal leaders.
On the third day of the truce, Gentius surrendered to Anicius in the Roman camp.
Anicius gave Gentius a dinner with full honors.
Anicius put Gentius under arrest after the dinner.
The Illyrians in Scodra surrendered.
The Illyrians in Scodra released the Roman envoys.
The Roman army marched north of Scutari Lake.
At Meteon, the Romans captured Gentius's queen, whom the campaign account calls Teuta.
The Romans captured Caravantius at Meteon.
The Romans captured Gentius's son Scerdilaides at Meteon.
The Romans captured Gentius's son Pleuratus at Meteon.
The Romans captured other leading Illyrians at Meteon.
Livy presents the fall of the Ardiaean state through a ceremonial account of Anicius's triumph in Rome.
The triumphal account says Anicius defeated the Illyrians on land and sea in a few days.
The triumphal account describes the Illyrians as brave.
The triumphal account says the Illyrians relied on their knowledge of the local terrain.
The triumphal account says the Illyrians also relied on their fortifications.
The campaign section gives thirty days as the length of the part of the campaign ending in Gentius's defeat.
Further Roman operations took place in the north of the Ardiaean state.
Anicius placed garrisons in some northern towns, citadels, and fortresses.
Issa, Rhizon, and Olcinium were among the cities where Anicius placed garrisons.
The tribal states of the Daorsi and the Pirustae also received Roman garrisons.
Some communities came over to Rome voluntarily.
Some places, including Pharos, were subdued by force.
Pharos and other places subdued by force had their property looted.
The booty shown in Rome's triumph included many captured royal flags.
The triumphal booty included Gentius's furniture.
The triumphal booty included Gentius's treasury.
The sale of booty brought in millions of sesterces.
The captured gold and silver went to the Roman state treasury.
The Roman Senate initially sent Gentius and his family to Spoletum to be kept under watch.
The other captives were imprisoned in Rome.
The inhabitants of Spoletum refused to keep the royal family under watch.
Spoletum's refusal prompted the transfer of the royal family to Iguvium.
The booty seized in Illyria included 220 vessels.
The Senate ordered that the captured vessels be given away.
C. Cassius Longinus distributed the vessels to the inhabitants of Corcyra, Apollonia, and Epidamnus.
Some surviving ruins may be Gentius's tomb.
Rome spared only the Illyrian koina that had openly supported it in the war.
Rome burned the cities, buildings, and public institutions of its Illyrian enemies.
Rome also thoroughly looted the communities that had opposed it.
The communities Rome spared retained their previous form of administration.
Spared communities continued to elect officials annually.
The spared communities paid Rome half the taxes they had paid to Gentius.
Rome dissolved the federation-based koina.
Each former unit was recognized as a separate koinon.
The separate koina had local autonomy.
The separate koina often had the right to mint their own coins.
The conquest of the southern Illyrian lands was permanent.
Roman legions continued trying to conquer northern and eastern Illyrian territories for about another hundred years.
The archaeologist Hasan Ceka proposed that Bellus was a mistranscription of Ballaeus, also called Ballaios.
The identification of Bellus with Ballaios is linguistically problematic.
Some have accepted Ballaios as Gentius's successor.
In the proposed succession, Ballaios had friendly relations with Rome.
Ballaios is described as an Illyrian king of the Ardiaei.
Ballaios is attested only by his coins, not by literary or historical accounts.
One proposed reign for Ballaios is 167–135 BC, but other dates have been suggested.
Ballaios appears to have ruled at Rhizon after 168 BC.
Rhizon had been a stronghold of Queen Teuta.
The region was part of the Roman Republic in Ballaios's time.
The Ardiaean kingdom had already been dissolved following Gentius's defeat.
Ballaios appears to have had some rivalry with Pharos.
Ballaios's coins are abundant in the region.
The abundance of his coins suggests that Ballaios had considerable influence in the region.
Gentiana lutea was named in honor of Gentius.
The rest of the genus Gentiana takes its name from Gentius by extension.
The naming reflects a belief that Gentius discovered the herbs' tonic properties.
Gentius is pictured on the reverse of the Albanian 50 lekë coin.
The 50 lekë coin bearing Gentius was issued in 1996 and 2000.
Gentius is pictured on the obverse of the Albanian 2,000 lekë banknote.
The 2,000 lekë banknote bearing Gentius was issued in 2008.

question.text: What was Gentius's main political action during his reign?
quotes: Gentius was the last attested Illyrian king, ruling from 181 to 168 BC from Scodra, in present-day Albania. Initially allied with Rome, he switched sides in 169 BC and joined Perseus of Macedon.

Gentius ruled the Illyrian kingdom from 181 to 168 BC and was its last attested king. Son of Pleuratus III, who had maintained friendly relations with Rome, he initially allied with Rome against Macedon in 171 BC.
